title: Sita insists

cards: Rama finds Sita in their rooms, still dressed for the coronation. He tells her. Then he tells her what he's decided for her: stay here in the palace, where you're safe.
Honor my father. Be kind to Bharata. Wait for me.
He describes the forest, to make sure she understands. Thorns on the paths. Lions and snakes.
Cold nights on the bare ground. Hunger, heat, wind. No place for a princess.

teach.h: I'LL WALK AHEAD, ON THE THORNS.
teach.b: In Valmiki's Ramayana, Sita doesn't answer quietly. A wife shares her husband's fortune, whatever it is, she tells him.

If you're going into the forest today, I'll go ahead of you and walk down the thorns and the sharp grass, so your path is softer. With you, the forest is a palace. He keeps refusing, so she gets sharper.
She asks, in effect, whether her father married her to someone with a man's shape but not a man's courage, if he'll leave his wife behind out of fear. She weeps. And Rama gives in.
She comes. Notice who wins this argument. Sita isn't following orders; she's overruling them.
The prince who calmly accepted exile from his father can't win an argument with his wife.
The tradition calls a wife sahadharmini: the one who shares dharma. Sita takes that literally. His path of dharma is her path too, and she won't let him walk it alone.
You can still see this at a Hindu wedding.
The couple circle the sacred fire together and take seven steps, the saptapadi, and the old words say, roughly: with these seven steps, be my friend.
Partners, not owner and follower. People read Sita's scene in more than one way. Some see the model of devotion in marriage.
Others hear, especially in that sharp line, a woman with her own will, choosing her own life. Both readings live in the tradition.
Neighbors have a line like it: in the Hebrew Bible, Ruth tells her mother-in-law that where she goes, Ruth will go.

how: Many Hindus honor Sita as a model of loyalty and strength; her insistence on going into exile is retold at weddings, in Ramlila, and in women's songs across India.

o: Sita begs Rama to fight for his father's throne
Sita refuses to stay behind and joins the exile
Sita agrees to wait for Rama in the palace

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: Sita stays safe in the palace
I'll walk ahead, on the thorns

s: Sita quietly obeys Rama and goes along
she argues, sharply, and overrules his plan to leave her behind.
Sita offers to walk ahead and tread down the thorns
so his path in the forest is softer.
there's only one way to read this scene
some see devotion in marriage; others see a woman choosing her own life. both readings live in the tradition.

games.q: you're Sita. your husband says you'll be safer in the palace for fourteen years without him. what do you do?
o: stay and wait, as he asks.
argue until he agrees you're coming.
go back to your father's house.
games.why: she argues, weeps, and even stings him with a sharp question, until he gives in. she goes into the forest beside him.

practice: Picture someone whose path you share: a partner, a sibling, a friend, a child. Walk seven slow steps, in your room or in your head, and with each one, name one thing you'd carry for them.
Then ask the harder question: who would walk into a forest for you? If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, just let their face come.

wordCard.voice: Sita insists. Told to stay safe in the palace, she argues her way into exile beside Rama: his path is hers.

orig.note: Sanskrit: she who shares (saha) dharma, a traditional word for a wife.

carryVoice: Your line: sahadharmini, partners in dharma. Sita's path was hers too, and she argued her way onto it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 26–30 (Rama tells Sita to stay; Sita's argument)
Grihya Sutras on the wedding rite, e.g. Paraskara Grihya Sutra 1.8 (the seven steps; 'with seven steps, be my friend')
